claims.source: The genotoxic impact of CPT and Etop is a well-documented consequence of their ability to trap (i.e., 'poison') respectively TOP1 and TOP2 cleavage complexes on the DNA, resulting in DNA damage (Pommier et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Inhibition of poly(ADP-ribose)polymerases 1–3 (PARP1-3) did not increase aggregation.
claims.source: Inhibition of poly(ADP-ribose)polymerases 1–3 (PARP1-3), involved in single-strand break repair, did not increase aggregation (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: PARP inhibition reduces the enhanced aggregation triggered by a loss of ATM.
claims.source: Recently, it was reported that PARP inhibition reduces the enhanced aggregation triggered by a loss of ATM (Lee et al., 2021), something we find as well for CPT-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Neither CPT nor Etop treatment in HEK293T cells had any effect on aggregation within the first 24 hr.
claims.source: Neither CPT nor Etop treatment in HEK293T cells had any effect on aggregation within the first 24 hr (Figure 1G and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The increased aggregation occurs only late after genotoxic stress.
claims.source: This reveals that the increased aggregation occurs only late and argues that it does not stem from any immediate, unknown damaging effect of either CPT or Etop on mRNA or protein molecules.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the time-course experimental data.

claims.claim: The increased protein aggregation triggered by targeting ATM, ATR, and TOPs is a late consequence of genotoxic stress.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that the increased protein aggregation triggered by targeting ATM, ATR, and TOPs is a late consequence of genotoxic stress.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing time-dependent effects.

claims.claim: 122 proteins aggregated significantly more after CPT treatment compared to control in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Using a stringent cutoff (Benjamini–Hochberg corrected p<0.05; –1>log2fold change >1; identified in >1 repeats of CPT-treated cells), we determined that 122 proteins aggregated significantly more after CPT treatment compared to only 29 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: 29 proteins aggregated significantly less after CPT treatment compared to control in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Using a stringent cutoff (Benjamini–Hochberg corrected p<0.05; –1>log2fold change >1; identified in >1 repeats of CPT-treated cells), we determined that 122 proteins aggregated significantly more after CPT treatment compared to only 29 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Most proteins that aggregate more after CPT treatment were not identified as aggregating in untreated cells.
claims.source: Most of them were not identified as aggregating in untreated cells, implying that they are soluble under normal conditions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: 39 proteins aggregated significantly more in ATM-inhibited HEK293T cells compared to control cells.
claims.source: We detected 39 proteins that aggregated significantly more in ATM-inhibited cells compared to control cells and 5 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: 5 proteins aggregated significantly less in ATM-inhibited HEK293T cells compared to control cells.
claims.source: We detected 39 proteins that aggregated significantly more in ATM-inhibited cells compared to control cells and 5 proteins that aggregated less (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Only one protein was found to aggregate more after both CPT treatment and inhibition of ATM in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Surprisingly, only one protein was found to aggregate more after both CPT treatment and inhibition of ATM (Figure 2C), suggesting that these genotoxic conditions drive the aggregation of different proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 aggregate more in CPT-treated HEK293 cells.
claims.source: We selected MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1, three proteins that were identified in our MS/MS analysis, to consistently aggregate more in CPT-treated HEK293T cells but that were not picked up in the ATM inhibition MS/MS analysis and confirmed that all three aggregated more in CPT-treated HEK293 cells (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claims.claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 aggregate more after treatment of HEK293 cells with ATM inhibitor.
claims.source: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 also aggregated more than in unstressed conditions after treatment of HEK293 cells with ATM inhibitor or when ATM was knocked out completely (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claims.claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 aggregate more in ATM knockout HEK293 cells.
claims.source: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 also aggregated more than in unstressed conditions after treatment of HEK293 cells with ATM inhibitor or when ATM was knocked out completely (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claims.claim: 210 proteins aggregated more in ATM KO U2OS cells.
claims.source: We found 210 proteins that aggregated more in ATM KO cells, while 53 proteins aggregated less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: 53 proteins aggregated less in ATM KO U2OS cells.
claims.source: We found 210 proteins that aggregated more in ATM KO cells, while 53 proteins aggregated less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: 114 of the 210 proteins that aggregate more in ATM KO U2OS cells were also found to aggregate more in ATM-depleted U2OS cells in a previous study.
claims.source: Of these 210 proteins, 114 were also found to aggregate more in ATM-depleted U2OS cells in a recent study by Lee et al., 2021.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited study.

claims.claim: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 106 proteins aggregating more.
claims.source: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 106 proteins aggregating more and 61 proteins to aggregate less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 61 proteins aggregating less.
claims.source: Treatment of U2OS cells with CPT resulted in 106 proteins aggregating more and 61 proteins to aggregate less (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Close to 20% of proteins that aggregated more after CPT treatment also aggregated in ATM KO U2OS cells.
claims.source: Close to 20% of proteins that aggregated more after CPT treatment also aggregated in ATM KO U2OS cells (20/106) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO or CPT-treated cells appear to be largely soluble in wild-type cells.
claims.source: Similar to the induced aggregation in HEK293T cells, proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO or CPT-treated cells appear to be largely soluble in wild-type cells, but now aggregate consistently (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Not a single protein was found to aggregate more in all four different conditions (HEK293T CPT, HEK293T ATM inhibitor, U2OS CPT, U2OS ATM KO).
claims.source: Not a single protein was found to aggregate more in all four different conditions, only two proteins aggregated more in both HEK293T and U2OS cells after CPT treatment, and only one protein overlapped between ATM KO U2OS cells and ATM-inhibited HEK293T cells (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Cytoskeleton-related GO terms are enriched across the different aggregating proteomes.
claims.source: Cytoskeleton-related terms, including microtubule and microfibril, are enriched across the different aggregating proteomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregated more in CPT-treated HEK293T cells are enriched for nucleotide binding terms, most prominently RNA binding.
claims.source: For example, proteins that aggregated more in CPT-treated HEK293T cells are enriched for nucleotide binding terms, most prominently RNA binding, which is highly enriched among proteins that aggregate after ATM inhibition as well (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: CPT treatment in HEK293T cells drives the aggregation of mitochondrial components.
claims.source: Specifically CPT treatment in HEK293T cells drives the aggregation of mitochondrial components (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: In U2OS cells, proteins that aggregate more after a loss of ATM or CPT treatment appear to be enriched for components involved in cell-cell contact, including cell adhesion and cellular membrane processes.
claims.source: In U2OS cells, proteins that aggregate more after a loss of ATM or CPT treatment appear to be enriched for components involved in cell-cell contact, including cell adhesion and cellular membrane processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: 66% (118/179) of the HEK293T baseline aggregating fraction aggregates in the U2OS baseline as well.
claims.source: This revealed that 66% (118/179) of the HEK293T baseline fraction aggregates in the U2OS baseline as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: 62% (99/160) of the proteins that aggregated more in CPT- or ATM inhibitor-treated HEK293T cells are also part of the U2OS baseline aggregation.
claims.source: Importantly, 62% (99/160) of the proteins that aggregated more in CPT- or ATM inhibitor-treated HEK293T cells are also part of the U2OS baseline (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: In unstressed U2OS cells protein aggregation is substantially more prominent than in untreated HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Indeed, silver staining revealed that in unstressed U2OS cells protein aggregation is substantially more prominent than in untreated HEK293T cells (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claims.claim: MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1 all aggregate strongly already in untreated wild-type U2OS cells.
claims.source: This is also reflected in MCM7, TUBA1A, and HDAC1, all three of which aggregate strongly already in (untreated) wild-type U2OS cells (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claims.claim: Aggregated proteins have in general a slightly lower or equal intrinsic propensity to aggregate compared to NIA proteins.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that aggregated proteins have in general a slightly lower (for the baseline aggregation) or equal (for CPT- and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation) intrinsic propensity to aggregate compared to NIA proteins (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TANGO and CamSol analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregate in CPT- or ATM-inhibited-treated HEK293T cells are in general highly abundant compared to NIA proteins.
claims.source: Interestingly, our MS/MS analysis revealed that proteins that aggregate in CPT- or ATM-inhibited-treated HEK293T cells are in general highly abundant compared to NIA proteins in (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: Genes coding for the aggregating proteins are in general higher expressed than genes coding for NIA proteins.
claims.source: After performing RNA sequencing on the same HEK293T cell samples that we used for our MS/MS analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2), we found that genes coding for the aggregating proteins are in general higher expressed than genes coding for NIA proteins (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: Aggregating proteins are in general more supersaturated than NIA proteins.
claims.source: Using the RNA-sequencing data (Supplementary file 2), we confirmed that aggregating proteins are in general indeed more supersaturated than NIA proteins (Figure 3D–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by supersaturation analysis using RNA-seq and TANGO data.

claims.claim: Most supersaturated proteins did not become SDS-insoluble, even after treatment with CPT or ATM inhibition.
claims.source: Although the relative supersaturation of aggregating proteins in HEK293T cells is intriguing, our data also indicates that most supersaturated proteins did not become SDS-insoluble, even after treatment with CPT or ATM inhibition (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the supersaturation analysis.

claims.claim: HEK293T baseline aggregation and both CPT- and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are made up of proteins that have a higher average LLPS propensity than NIA proteins.
claims.source: Using catGRANULE (Mitchell et al., 2013; http://tartaglialab.com), we find that HEK293T baseline aggregation and both CPT- and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are indeed made up of proteins that have a higher average LLPS propensity than NIA proteins (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by catGRANULE analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: HEK293T baseline and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are enriched for proteins that have a high propensity to engage in LLPS-relevant pi-pi interactions.
claims.source: HEK293T baseline and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation are also enriched for proteins that have a high propensity to engage in LLPS-relevant pi-pi interactions, as indicated by both a higher average PScore and a larger percentage of proteins that have a PScore > 4 (i.e., above the threshold defined by Vernon et al., 2018; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PScore analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: Baseline aggregation in U2OS cells is made up of supersaturated, LLPS-prone proteins.
claims.source: Upon examining the proteins that aggregate in U2OS cells, we found further support for this. Baseline aggregation in U2OS cells is also made up of supersaturated, LLPS-prone proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–R).
claims.evidence: This is supported by supersaturation and LLPS propensity analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: Many supersaturated proteins are not SDS-insoluble in U2OS cells, even in cells treated with CPT or in cells lacking ATM.
claims.source: Despite the baseline aggregation being far more pronounced in U2OS cells than in HEK293T cells, many supersaturated proteins are not SDS-insoluble in U2OS cells, even in cells treated with CPT or in cells lacking ATM (Figure 3—figure supplement 1O).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the supersaturation analysis.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO cells are supersaturated compared to U2OS NIA proteins.
claims.source: In U2OS ATM KO cells, proteins that aggregate more are supersaturated compared to U2OS NIA proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M); for CPT-treated cells, this is not the case (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M–O).
claims.evidence: This is supported by supersaturation analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO cells have a higher general propensity to engage in LLPS as predicted by PScore and catGRANULE.
claims.source: Proteins that aggregate more in U2OS ATM KO cells also have a higher general propensity to engage in LLPS as predicted by PScore and catGRANULE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1P and Q), while proteins that aggregate more in CPT-treated cells are enriched for proteins with a PScore > 4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1R).
claims.evidence: This is supported by PScore and catGRANULE analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: Only two transcripts were significantly altered after ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells despite the enhanced aggregation occurring in these cells.
claims.source: Intriguingly, only two transcripts (one up and one down) were significantly altered (–1 > log2FC > 1) after ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells despite the enhanced aggregation occurring in these cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: The enhanced aggregation after CPT treatment or a loss of ATM function is mostly driven by the physicochemical characteristics of the proteins involved.
claims.source: This further underlines that the enhanced aggregation after CPT treatment or a loss of ATM function is mostly driven by the physicochemical characteristics of the proteins involved.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcriptional changes and the supersaturation/LLPS propensity data.

claims.claim: The consistent aggregation of vulnerable proteins across independent repeats argues against the possibility that this is caused by any genotoxic stress-induced DNA sequence alterations in their own coding regions.
claims.source: Their consistent aggregation across independent repeats argues against the possibility that this is caused by any genotoxic stress-induced DNA sequence alterations in their own coding regions as these would occur more randomly throughout the genome.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the consistency of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: The increased aggregation cannot be explained by any changes in abundance of the proteins involved.
claims.source: Moreover, we find that the increased aggregation can also not be explained by any changes in abundance of the proteins involved, resulting for example from DNA damage-induced transcriptional dysregulation, as very limited overlap exists between proteins that aggregate and proteins with an altered expression upon CPT treatment or ATM loss (see Figure 4A for HEK293T and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A for U2OS).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of MS/MS and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: A long-term consequence of genotoxic conditions is a global lowering of the aggregation threshold of proteins.
claims.source: Instead, our data indicate that a long-term consequence of these genotoxic conditions is a global lowering of the aggregation threshold of proteins.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing widespread aggregation of metastable proteins.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregate more in HEK293T and U2OS cells after CPT treatment or after a loss of ATM are enriched for proteins that have been reported to aggregate upon heat treatment of cells.
claims.source: In line with this, we find that proteins that aggregate more in HEK293T and U2OS cells after CPT treatment or after a (functional) loss of ATM are enriched for proteins that have been reported to aggregate upon heat treatment of cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; Mymrikov et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited heat stress aggregation dataset.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregate more after genotoxic stress are enriched for constituents of stress granules.
claims.source: In addition, they are enriched for constituents of stress granules (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; http://rnagranuledb.lunenfeld.ca), cellular condensates that have been found to function as nucleation sites for protein aggregation (Dobra et al., 2018; Mateju et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with a stress granule database and citations.

claims.claim: Protein synthesis is reduced approximately threefold in CPT-treated cells.
claims.source: Notably, protein synthesis is reduced approximately threefold in CPT-treated cells (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by radioactive pulse labeling data.

claims.claim: Radioactively labeled proteins were present in the aggregating fraction of CPT-treated cells but were not enriched compared to control cells.
claims.source: Despite this strong reduction in protein synthesis, radioactively labeled proteins were still clearly present in the aggregating fraction of CPT-treated cells. They were however not enriched in the aggregating fraction compared to control cells (Figure 4D), indicating that the enhanced aggregation triggered by CPT is not explained through an accelerated aggregation of specifically newly synthesized proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by radioactive pulse labeling data.

claims.claim: Proteins that aggregate after transient CPT treatment are enriched for constituents of various disease-associated protein aggregates.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we find that proteins that aggregate after transient CPT treatment are enriched for constituents of various disease-associated protein aggregates (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with disease-associated aggregation datasets.

claims.claim: 67% (82/122) of proteins that aggregate after CPT treatment have been previously identified in TDP-43 aggregates, Lewy bodies, α-synuclein-induced aggregates, or found to aggregate in Huntington's disease or Alzheimer's disease brains.
claims.source: 67% (82/122) of them – or their mouse homologs – have already previously been identified in TDP-43 aggregates (Dammer et al., 2012; Zuo et al., 2021), Lewy bodies (McCormack et al., 2019), or α-synuclein-induced aggregates (Mahul-Mellier et al., 2020), or found to aggregate in Huntington's disease (HD) (Hosp et al., 2017) or Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains (Hales et al., 2016; Kepchia et al., 2020 Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited disease-associated aggregation datasets.

claims.claim: Transient targeting of ATM, ATR, and TOPs accelerates polyQ aggregation in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: Transient targeting of ATM, ATR, and in particular TOPs, but not TDP1, 24–48 hr prior to the expression of polyQ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) indeed accelerated polyQ aggregation in these cells (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), closely mirroring the increased aggregation that we observed before (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by filter trap assay data.

claims.claim: The accelerated polyQ aggregation under genotoxic conditions is dose-dependent.
claims.source: The accelerated polyQ aggregation under these conditions is also dose-dependent (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I), and it is not explained by changes in total polyQ levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by filter trap assay and Western blot data.

claims.claim: The accelerated polyQ aggregation induced by genotoxic conditions cannot be explained by an exacerbated repeat instability.
claims.source: Importantly, we find no evidence that the accelerated polyQ aggregation induced by these genotoxic conditions can be explained by an exacerbated repeat instability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CAG repeat length analysis data.

claims.claim: Transient targeting of either ATM or TOP1 results in an enrichment of luciferase-GFP in the aggregated fraction.
claims.source: We find that transient targeting of either ATM or TOP1 results in an enrichment of luciferase-GFP in the aggregated fraction (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data.

claims.claim: ATM inhibition and CPT treatment result in increased aggregation of multiple (co)chaperones in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: We noted that ATM inhibition and in particular CPT treatment resulted in an increased aggregation of multiple (co)chaperones in HEK293T cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: In U2OS cells, many (co)chaperones are already aggregating regardless of exposure to genotoxic stress.
claims.source: In U2OS cells, many (co)chaperones are already aggregating regardless of exposure to genotoxic stress, but still several chaperones aggregated significantly more in ATM KO cells or in cells treated with CPT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS proteomics data.

claims.claim: HSPA8 and HSPA1A clients are enriched among aggregating proteins.
claims.source: Upon cross-referencing the NIA and aggregating fractions against a recently generated client database of HSPA8 (HSC70; constitutively active form of HSP70) and HSPA1A (constitutively active and stress-inducible HSP70) (Ryu et al., 2020), we find that HSPA8 and HSPA1A clients are enriched among aggregating proteins (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited client database.

claims.claim: All aggregating fractions are enriched for (co)chaperone interactors compared to nonaggregating proteins.
claims.source: We find that all aggregating fractions are enriched for (co)chaperone interactors compared to nonaggregating proteins (NIA) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by BioGRID interaction database analysis.

claims.claim: Treatment with CPT results in an overall upward shift of (co)chaperone expression levels in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: In HEK293T cells, we find that treatment with CPT results in an overall upward shift of (co)chaperone expression levels, as measured in both our WCL MS/MS analysis (16 up, 8 down) (Figure 5E) and in our RNAseq dataset (11 up, 5 down) (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by MS/MS and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: HSF1 is partially activated by CPT treatment in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: HSF1 is indeed partially activated by CPT treatment in HEK293T cells (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing HSF1 phosphorylation.

claims.claim: ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells resulted in a marginal HSF1 activation.
claims.source: ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells resulted in a marginal HSF1 activation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data.

claims.claim: Gene expression levels of Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells.
claims.source: For example, we found that gene expression levels of the small heat shock-like protein Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells, gene expression levels of the stress-inducible HSPA1A are >150-fold higher, and that of HSPB5 (or CRYAB, i.e., αB-crystallin) were >400-fold higher.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Gene expression levels of HSPA1A are >150-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells.
claims.source: For example, we found that gene expression levels of the small heat shock-like protein Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells, gene expression levels of the stress-inducible HSPA1A are >150-fold higher, and that of HSPB5 (or CRYAB, i.e., αB-crystallin) were >400-fold higher.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Gene expression levels of HSPB5 are >400-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells.
claims.source: For example, we found that gene expression levels of the small heat shock-like protein Clusterin (CLU) are >100-fold higher in wild-type U2OS compared to HEK293T cells, gene expression levels of the stress-inducible HSPA1A are >150-fold higher, and that of HSPB5 (or CRYAB, i.e., αB-crystallin) were >400-fold higher.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Mild HSP70 inhibition using VER-155008 after CPT treatment increased CPT-induced protein aggregation.
claims.source: Indeed, mild HSP70 inhibition using the HSP70/HSC70 inhibitor VER-155008 after CPT treatment increased CPT-induced protein aggregation even further, while having no clear impact on aggregation in control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claims.claim: Overexpression of HSPB5 drastically reduced the enhanced protein aggregation in U2OS ATM KO cells.
claims.source: We generated U2OS cells that stably overexpress HSPB5 in both wild-type and ATM-deficient backgrounds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), and confirmed that this drastically reduced the enhanced protein aggregation in the latter (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silver staining and quantification data.

claims.claim: HSPB5 overexpression reduced ProteoStat aggresome staining in U2OS ATM KO cells.
claims.source: HSPB5 overexpression also reduced ProteoStat aggresome staining and the occurrence of cytoplasmic FUS puncta (without affecting overall FUS levels; see Supplementary file 1), two other markers of a disrupted protein homeostasis (Figure 6D–G; Neumann et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: HSPB5 overexpression reduced the occurrence of cytoplasmic FUS puncta in U2OS ATM KO cells.
claims.source: HSPB5 overexpression also reduced ProteoStat aggresome staining and the occurrence of cytoplasmic FUS puncta (without affecting overall FUS levels; see Supplementary file 1), two other markers of a disrupted protein homeostasis (Figure 6D–G; Neumann et al., 2006; Shen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: Gamma irradiation-induced DNA lesion accumulation and subsequent resolution as measured by 53BP1 foci formation was not affected by HSPB5 expression in U2OS wild-type or ATM KO cells.
claims.source: However, we found no indication for this as the gamma irradiation-induced DNA lesion accumulation and subsequent resolution as measured by 53BP1 foci formation was not affected by HSPB5 expression in neither U2OS wild-type nor ATM KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: Neither HSPB5, nor HSP70 nor HSP90 accumulated at CPT- or gamma irradiation-induced DNA damage sites.
claims.source: Moreover, neither HSPB5, nor HSP70 nor HSP90 accumulated at either CPT- or gamma irradiation-induced DNA damage sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: The overload of chaperones is not due to a sequestering to DNA damage sites.
claims.source: This points out that the overload of chaperones is not due to a sequestering to DNA damage sites.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of chaperone accumulation at DNA damage sites.

claims.claim: Overexpression of HSPB5 can reduce the enhanced protein aggregation in CPT-treated U2OS cells.
claims.source: Crucially, we found that overexpression of HSPB5 can reduce the enhanced protein aggregation in CPT-treated U2OS cells as well (Figure 6H, I), but that stable overexpression of HSPB5 has no effect on the CPT-induced aggregation in HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claims.claim: Stable overexpression of HSPB5 has no effect on the CPT-induced aggregation in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: Crucially, we found that overexpression of HSPB5 can reduce the enhanced protein aggregation in CPT-treated U2OS cells as well (Figure 6H, I), but that stable overexpression of HSPB5 has no effect on the CPT-induced aggregation in HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silver staining data.

claims.claim: TOP poisoning and functional impairment of ATM or ATR trigger a widespread aggregation of LLPS-prone and supersaturated proteins.
claims.source: Here, we report that TOP poisoning and functional impairment of ATM or ATR trigger a widespread aggregation of LLPS-prone and supersaturated proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The aggregation of metastable proteins is a consequence of an overload of chaperone systems under genotoxic conditions.
claims.source: Our data show that the aggregation of these metastable proteins is a consequence of an overload of chaperone systems under these genotoxic conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and inference.

claims.claim: CPT treatment leads to a strong reduction in protein synthesis over time.
claims.source: It is further supported by the notion that CPT treatment leads to a strong reduction in protein synthesis over time, something that has been reported for other forms of DNA damage as well (Halim et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation.

claims.claim: Reduced protein synthesis is a well-known response to proteotoxic stress and is believed to lower the strong demand for chaperone capacity of nascent chains.
claims.source: Reduced protein synthesis is a well-known response to proteotoxic stress and is believed to lower the strong demand for chaperone capacity of nascent chains that are innately vulnerable to misfolding and aggregation (Balchin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Despite a reduction in protein synthesis, genotoxic stress still leads to an overload of chaperone systems.
claims.source: This indicates that despite a reduction in protein synthesis, genotoxic stress still leads to an overload of chaperone systems, causing protein homeostasis to shift.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced synthesis but increased aggregation.

claims.claim: The shift in protein homeostasis after genotoxic stress is reminiscent of what occurs under conditions of chronic stress.
claims.source: The observed shift in protein homeostasis after genotoxic stress is strikingly reminiscent of what is believed to occur under conditions of (chronic) stress (Weids et al., 2016) and during many age-related neurodegenerative disorders (David et al., 2010; Hipp et al., 2019; Morley et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claims.claim: Supersaturated proteins have been found to be overrepresented in cellular pathways associated with neurodegenerative disorders.
claims.source: Supersaturated proteins have been found to be overrepresented in cellular pathways associated with these disorders (Ciryam et al., 2015), and disease-associated aggregating proteins, including FUS, tau, and α-synuclein, are known to exhibit LLPS behavior (reviewed in Zbinden et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The shift in protein homeostasis under genotoxic stress conditions can be caused by either an altered capacity of protein quality control systems or by an increased demand emanating from an altered proteome.
claims.source: The shift in protein homeostasis under genotoxic stress conditions can theoretically be caused by either an altered capacity of protein quality control systems or by an increased demand emanating from an altered proteome.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claims.claim: The overload of chaperone systems is largely caused by an increased demand for chaperone activity in the proteome.
claims.source: Nevertheless, our data lead us to hypothesize that the overload of chaperone systems is largely caused by an increased demand for chaperone activity in the proteome.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The strong upregulation of several small heat shock proteins in U2OS cells points at a rewiring of the chaperone network towards a more prominent reliance on this class of chaperones.
claims.source: The strong upregulation of several small heat shock (-like) proteins in U2OS cells, including HSPB5, seems to point at a rewiring of the chaperone network in this cell line towards a more prominent reliance on this class of chaperones.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing differential chaperone expression.

claims.claim: Cancer cells inherently exhibit elevated levels of protein stress, which has been attributed to an increased protein folding and degradation demand.
claims.source: Cancer cells inherently exhibit elevated levels of protein stress, which has been attributed to an increased protein folding and degradation demand (Dai et al., 2012; Deshaies, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Any increased demand caused by genotoxic conditions is independent of quantitative changes of the aggregating proteins themselves and likely also of any genetic alterations in their coding regions.
claims.source: Our data indicate that any increased demand caused by these genotoxic conditions is, however independent of quantitative changes of the aggregating proteins themselves and likely also of any genetic alterations in their coding regions (in cis genetic alterations).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between aggregation and protein/transcript abundance changes.

claims.claim: During proteomic stress a destabilization of the background proteome can result in a competition for the limited chaperone capacity available.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that during proteomic stress a destabilization of the background proteome can result in a competition for the limited chaperone capacity available, causing proteins that are highly dependent on chaperones for their stability and solubility to aggregate readily (Gidalevitz et al., 2010; Gidalevitz et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The aggregation that occurs after genotoxic stress is enriched for RNA-binding proteins.
claims.source: Strikingly, we find that the aggregation that occurs after genotoxic stress is enriched for RNA-binding proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of the MS/MS data.

claims.claim: The enhanced aggregation after genotoxic stress can be mitigated by inhibiting PARylation.
claims.source: This enhanced aggregation can also be mitigated by inhibiting PARylation, which plays a key role in the regulation of LLPS processes (Duan et al., 2019; McGurk et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claims.claim: Aberrant LLPS can drive the nucleation of insoluble protein aggregates.
claims.source: LLPS is a different biochemical process than protein aggregation (with different underlying mechanisms and principles), but aberrant LLPS can drive the nucleation of insoluble (fibrillar) protein aggregates, for example, for polyQ (Peskett et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Chaperones, and in particular small heat shock proteins, play a pivotal role in the surveillance of biomolecular condensates.
claims.source: Although data is so far limited, chaperones, and in particular small heat shock proteins, have been reported to play a pivotal role in the surveillance of biomolecular condensates.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claims.claim: The HSPB8-BAG3-HSPA1A complex is important for maintaining stress granule dynamics.
claims.source: For example, the HSPB8-BAG3-HSPA1A complex has been found to be important for maintaining stress granule dynamics (Ganassi et al., 2016), and recent work uncovered that HSPB1 is important to prevent aberrant phase transitions of FUS (Liu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: HSPB1 is important to prevent aberrant phase transitions of FUS.
claims.source: For example, the HSPB8-BAG3-HSPA1A complex has been found to be important for maintaining stress granule dynamics (Ganassi et al., 2016), and recent work uncovered that HSPB1 is important to prevent aberrant phase transitions of FUS (Liu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: HSPB5 has been found to associate with nuclear speckles.
claims.source: Interestingly, although HSPB5 itself has so far not been shown to undergo LLPS, like HSPB1, it has been found to associate with nuclear speckles (van den IJssel et al., 1998), which are membraneless as well.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: HSPB5 is important to maintain the stability of the cytoskeleton.
claims.source: HSPB5 has also been shown to be important to maintain the stability of the cytoskeleton (Ghosh et al., 2007; Golenhofen et al., 1999; Yin et al., 2019), and we find that many proteins that aggregate upon genotoxic stress conditions are cytoskeleton (-related) components.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cytoskeleton organization is regulated through LLPS processes.
claims.source: A growing body of evidence indicates that cytoskeleton organization is regulated through LLPS processes (reviewed in Wiegand and Hyman, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Genotoxic stress conditions can exacerbate the risk of aberrant progression of LLPS processes.
claims.source: Our data thus indicate that genotoxic stress conditions can exacerbate the risk of aberrant progression of LLPS processes, which in turn may trigger an overload of chaperone systems.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing LLPS-prone protein aggregation.

claims.claim: The increased protein aggregation that occurs after a loss of ATM has been recently attributed to an accumulation of DNA damage.
claims.source: The increased protein aggregation that occurs after a loss of ATM – including in A-T patient brains – has been recently attributed to an accumulation of DNA damage (Lee et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: An impaired response to DNA damage is believed to be the primary driving force of A-T phenotypes.
claims.source: As an impaired response to DNA damage is believed to be the primary driving force of A-T phenotypes (Shiloh, 2020), these findings have fueled the idea that a disruption of protein homeostasis may be an important disease mechanism in A-T.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The widespread aggregation caused by a loss of ATM follows a predictable pattern that overlaps with the aggregation believed to underlie many neurodegenerative disorders.
claims.source: Our data provide further support for this as they show that the widespread aggregation caused by a loss of ATM follows a predictable pattern that overlaps strikingly with the aggregation that is believed to underlie many neurodegenerative disorders.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing overlap with disease-associated aggregation.

claims.claim: Other genotoxic conditions, including chemotherapeutic TOP poisons, can have a very similar impact on protein aggregation as loss of ATM.
claims.source: Importantly, our findings also provide a proof of principle that other genotoxic conditions – including chemotherapeutic TOP poisons – can have a very similar impact.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing similar aggregation patterns.

claims.claim: There exists a broader link between DNA damage and a loss of protein homeostasis.
claims.source: This points at the existence of a broader link between DNA damage and a loss of protein homeostasis .
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing multiple genotoxic conditions trigger aggregation.

results.result: Genotoxic stress induced by ATM knockout, ATM inhibition, ATR inhibition, and topoisomerase poisoning (CPT and etoposide) causes increased protein aggregation in both U2OS and HEK293 cell lines. This aggregation is dose-dependent, occurs late (after 24 hours), and is a consequence of genotoxic stress rather than immediate drug effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C36 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (knockout, chemical inhibition, different drugs) showing consistent increases in protein aggregation. The time-course data (C34-C36) and dose-response relationships (C30) strengthen the conclusion that this is a late, specific consequence of genotoxic stress. The data are supported by silver staining and Western blot analyses across multiple independent experiments.

results.result: Proteomics analysis reveals that CPT treatment and ATM inhibition trigger aggregation of distinct but overlapping sets of proteins in HEK293T and U2OS cells. In HEK293T, 122 proteins aggregate more after CPT treatment and 39 after ATM inhibition, with minimal overlap. In U2OS, 210 proteins aggregate more in ATM KO cells and 106 after CPT treatment, with ~20% overlap. Cell-type-specific differences are substantial, with many proteins aggregating in one cell line but not the other.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C53 are supported by rigorous MS/MS proteomics with stringent statistical cutoffs (Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p<0.05, log2FC>1). The validation of specific proteins (MCM7, TUBA1A, HDAC1) by Western blot (C43-C45) confirms the MS/MS findings. The cell-type specificity is well-documented and reproducible across independent experiments.

results.result: GO term analysis reveals that aggregating proteins are enriched for cytoskeleton-related components across conditions, with additional cell-type and treatment-specific enrichments including RNA binding (HEK293T CPT/ATM inhibition), mitochondrial components (HEK293T CPT), and cell adhesion/membrane processes (U2OS).
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by systematic GO term analysis of the MS/MS data. The enrichments are statistically significant and consistent with the biological functions expected to be vulnerable to proteostatic stress. The cell-type specificity adds biological insight.

results.result: U2OS cells exhibit substantially higher baseline protein aggregation compared to HEK293T cells, with 66% of HEK293T baseline aggregating proteins also aggregating in U2OS. Importantly, 62% of proteins that aggregate after genotoxic stress in HEK293T are already part of the U2OS baseline aggregation, indicating a lower aggregation threshold in U2OS cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by MS/MS proteomics and silver staining data showing quantitative differences in baseline aggregation between cell lines. The overlap analysis is rigorous and the Western blot validation of specific proteins (MCM7, TUBA1A, HDAC1) confirms the cell-type differences. This provides important context for interpreting the genotoxic stress responses.

results.result: Aggregating proteins after genotoxic stress are characterized by high abundance and supersaturation rather than high intrinsic aggregation propensity. Proteins that aggregate have equal or slightly lower TANGO scores compared to non-aggregating proteins, but are expressed at higher levels (both protein and transcript) and are more supersaturated. However, most supersaturated proteins do not become insoluble even after genotoxic stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by comprehensive bioinformatics analysis combining MS/MS proteomics, RNA-seq, and computational predictions (TANGO, supersaturation calculations). The finding that intrinsic aggregation propensity is not elevated (C62) while abundance and supersaturation are increased (C63-C65) is counterintuitive but well-supported by the data. The observation that most supersaturated proteins remain soluble (C66) is an important caveat.

results.result: Aggregating proteins are enriched for liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) propensity as measured by catGRANULE scores and PScore analysis. This enrichment is observed in both HEK293T (baseline, CPT, and ATM inhibitor-induced aggregation) and U2OS cells (baseline and ATM KO-induced aggregation). LLPS propensity appears to discriminate which supersaturated proteins aggregate.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by systematic computational analysis using established LLPS prediction tools (catGRANULE, PScore). The statistical significance is demonstrated across multiple conditions and cell types. The finding that LLPS propensity distinguishes aggregating from non-aggregating supersaturated proteins (implicit in C67-C72) is biologically insightful and well-supported.

results.result: The enhanced aggregation after genotoxic stress is driven by physicochemical characteristics of proteins rather than transcriptional changes. Only two transcripts were significantly altered after ATM inhibition in HEK293T cells, and there is minimal overlap between proteins that aggregate and proteins with altered expression. The consistent aggregation of specific proteins across independent experiments argues against random DNA sequence alterations.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by RNA-seq data showing minimal transcriptional changes (C73) and lack of correlation between aggregation and expression changes (C76). The consistency across replicates (C75) is well-documented in the MS/MS data. This is a key mechanistic insight that the aggregation is not due to altered protein levels or genetic changes.

results.result: Genotoxic conditions cause a global lowering of the protein aggregation threshold, allowing metastable proteins that are normally soluble to aggregate.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 is a synthesis of the preceding findings (C62-C76) and is well-supported by the collective evidence showing that proteins with similar physicochemical properties aggregate consistently without changes in their own abundance or sequence. This represents the central mechanistic conclusion of the study.

results.result: Proteins that aggregate after genotoxic stress overlap significantly with proteins that aggregate under heat stress and with stress granule constituents, indicating similarity to classic proteotoxic stress responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by systematic comparison with published datasets (Mymrikov et al. 2017 for heat stress, RNA granule database for stress granules). The enrichment analysis is statistically significant and provides important biological context linking genotoxic stress to proteotoxic stress.

results.result: Protein synthesis is reduced approximately threefold in CPT-treated cells, but newly synthesized proteins are not preferentially enriched in the aggregating fraction compared to control cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by radioactive pulse-labeling experiments with appropriate controls. The finding that newly synthesized proteins are not enriched in aggregates despite being present (C81) is an important negative result that helps define the mechanism. The quantification appears rigorous with n=4 replicates.

results.result: Proteins that aggregate after CPT treatment are highly enriched for constituents of disease-associated protein aggregates, with 67% (82/122) previously identified in TDP-43 aggregates, Lewy bodies, α-synuclein-induced aggregates, or aggregates from Huntington's or Alzheimer's disease brains.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 are supported by systematic comparison with multiple published disease-associated aggregation datasets. The 67% overlap is substantial and statistically significant. This is a key finding linking genotoxic stress-induced aggregation to neurodegenerative disease mechanisms.

results.result: Genotoxic stress accelerates aggregation of polyglutamine (Q71) in a dose-dependent manner without increasing CAG repeat instability or total polyQ levels. Targeting ATM, ATR, and TOPs (but not TDP1) accelerates polyQ aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by filter trap assays with appropriate controls for protein levels and repeat length. The dose-dependence (C85) and exclusion of repeat instability as a mechanism (C86) strengthen the conclusion that this reflects a lowered aggregation threshold. The use of an established disease-relevant model substrate is appropriate.

results.result: Transient targeting of ATM or TOP1 results in enrichment of luciferase-GFP (a folding-sensitive model substrate) in the aggregated fraction.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by Western blot data showing enrichment of luciferase-GFP in aggregates. This provides additional evidence using a different model substrate that the aggregation threshold is lowered. However, only n=2 is noted, which is a limitation.

results.result: Multiple chaperones aggregate after genotoxic stress in both HEK293T (ATM inhibition and CPT treatment) and U2OS cells (baseline and increased after ATM KO or CPT treatment), with cell-type-specific patterns of chaperone aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by MS/MS proteomics data identifying specific chaperones in the aggregated fractions. The cell-type specificity is well-documented. This is important evidence for chaperone sequestration as a mechanism of chaperone overload.

results.result: Aggregating proteins are enriched for chaperone clients and interactors. HSPA8 and HSPA1A clients are enriched among aggregating proteins, and all aggregating fractions show enrichment for chaperone interactors compared to non-aggregating proteins based on BioGRID database analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by systematic cross-referencing with published client databases (Ryu et al. 2020) and BioGRID interaction data. The enrichment is statistically significant and provides evidence that aggregating proteins are normally chaperone-dependent. The authors appropriately note limitations of interaction databases for capturing transient chaperone-client interactions.

results.result: CPT treatment induces an upward shift in chaperone expression levels in HEK293T cells (16 up, 8 down by MS/MS; 11 up, 5 down by RNA-seq) accompanied by partial HSF1 activation. ATM inhibition results in only marginal HSF1 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by both MS/MS and RNA-seq data showing consistent upregulation of chaperones, and Western blot data showing HSF1 phosphorylation. The convergence of protein and transcript data strengthens the conclusion. The differential response to ATM inhibition vs CPT (C94) is an interesting observation.

results.result: U2OS cells express dramatically higher levels of specific chaperones compared to HEK293T cells: Clusterin (CLU) >100-fold, HSPA1A >150-fold, and HSPB5 >400-fold higher in U2OS.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by RNA-seq data comparing the two cell lines. The magnitude of differences is substantial and provides important context for understanding the different baseline aggregation states and responses to genotoxic stress in the two cell lines.

results.result: Mild HSP70 inhibition using VER-155008 after CPT treatment further increases CPT-induced protein aggregation without affecting aggregation in control cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by silver staining and Western blot data. This is important functional evidence that chaperone capacity is limiting and that further reducing it exacerbates aggregation. The specificity to CPT-treated cells (no effect in controls) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Stable overexpression of HSPB5 drastically reduces enhanced protein aggregation in U2OS ATM KO cells, as measured by silver staining, ProteoStat aggresome staining, and reduction of cytoplasmic FUS puncta.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by multiple complementary assays (silver staining, ProteoStat, immunofluorescence) showing consistent reduction in aggregation markers. The use of multiple readouts strengthens the conclusion. This is a key proof-of-principle that increasing chaperone capacity can rescue the aggregation phenotype.

results.result: HSPB5 overexpression does not affect DNA repair kinetics (53BP1 foci formation/resolution) in U2OS cells, and HSPB5, HSP70, and HSP90 do not accumulate at DNA damage sites, indicating that chaperone overload is not due to sequestration at DNA damage sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing no effect on DNA repair and no chaperone localization to damage sites. This is an important control experiment that rules out a direct role of chaperones in DNA repair and supports the conclusion that chaperone overload occurs through a different mechanism.

results.result: HSPB5 overexpression reduces enhanced protein aggregation in CPT-treated U2OS cells but has no effect on CPT-induced aggregation in HEK293 cells, demonstrating cell-type specificity of the rescue effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by silver staining data in both cell lines. The cell-type specificity is an important finding that relates to the different baseline chaperone expression profiles and aggregation states in the two cell lines. This suggests that the chaperone network context determines whether HSPB5 overexpression is effective.

results.result: TOP poisoning and functional impairment of ATM or ATR trigger widespread aggregation of LLPS-prone and supersaturated proteins as a consequence of chaperone system overload under genotoxic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 represent the central conclusions of the study, synthesizing the findings from C5-C106. These are well-supported by the collective evidence including proteomics, bioinformatics, functional assays with model substrates, and rescue experiments. The mechanistic link between genotoxic stress, chaperone overload, and aggregation of metastable proteins is convincingly demonstrated.

results.result: Despite a strong reduction in protein synthesis (a known response to proteotoxic stress that should reduce chaperone demand), genotoxic stress still leads to chaperone system overload and a shift in protein homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by the radioactive pulse-labeling data (C80-C81) and established knowledge about protein synthesis reduction during stress (C110). The inference that chaperone overload persists despite reduced synthesis (C111) is logical and well-supported, suggesting a substantial increase in chaperone demand.

results.result: The shift in protein homeostasis after genotoxic stress is reminiscent of chronic stress and age-related neurodegenerative disorders, where supersaturated proteins are overrepresented in disease-associated pathways and disease proteins exhibit LLPS behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are supported by comparison with cited literature on chronic stress and neurodegeneration. The similarity in protein characteristics (supersaturation, LLPS propensity) and overlap with disease-associated aggregates (C82-C83) support this conclusion. This places the findings in important biological context.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that chaperone system overload is largely caused by increased demand for chaperone activity in the proteome rather than altered chaperone capacity, though both mechanisms could contribute.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 represent a hypothesis rather than a definitive conclusion. While the data showing chaperone upregulation (C92-C93), chaperone aggregation (C88-C89), and enrichment of chaperone clients among aggregating proteins (C90-C91) support increased demand, the relative contributions of altered capacity vs. increased demand are not definitively quantified. The authors appropriately frame this as a hypothesis.

results.result: The strong upregulation of small heat shock proteins in U2OS cells points to a rewiring of the chaperone network toward greater reliance on this chaperone class.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by the RNA-seq data showing dramatic upregulation of small heat shock proteins in U2OS (C95-C97) and the effectiveness of HSPB5 overexpression in U2OS but not HEK293 cells (C105-C106). This is a reasonable inference about cell-type-specific chaperone network organization.

results.result: Cancer cells (U2OS) inherently exhibit elevated protein stress, and the increased chaperone demand from genotoxic conditions is independent of quantitative changes in aggregating proteins themselves or genetic alterations in their coding regions.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is established knowledge supported by citations. Claim C118 is supported by the lack of correlation between aggregation and expression changes (C76) and the consistency of aggregation across replicates (C75). This helps explain the cell-type differences and mechanism of aggregation.

results.result: The aggregation after genotoxic stress is enriched for RNA-binding proteins and can be mitigated by inhibiting PARylation, which regulates LLPS processes, suggesting a role for aberrant LLPS in the aggregation mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 is established knowledge. Claim C120 is supported by GO term analysis (C55). Claim C121 is supported by experimental data (C33) and citations linking PARylation to LLPS regulation. Together these support a mechanistic link between genotoxic stress, LLPS dysregulation, and protein aggregation.

results.result: Aberrant LLPS can drive protein aggregation, and chaperones (particularly small heat shock proteins like HSPB5 and HSPB1) play important roles in surveilling biomolecular condensates and preventing aberrant phase transitions. HSPB5 associates with nuclear speckles and maintains cytoskeleton stability, both of which involve LLPS processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C128 are established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. This provides important biological context for understanding why LLPS-prone proteins aggregate under genotoxic stress and why HSPB5 is effective at suppressing this aggregation. The connection to cytoskeleton (C127-C128) is relevant given the enrichment of cytoskeleton proteins in aggregates (C54).

results.result: Genotoxic stress conditions can exacerbate the risk of aberrant progression of LLPS processes, which may trigger chaperone system overload.
results.evaluation: Claim C129 is a synthesis of the findings showing LLPS-prone protein aggregation (C67-C72), enrichment of RNA-binding proteins (C120), and the role of PARylation (C121). This represents a mechanistic model linking genotoxic stress to LLPS dysregulation to chaperone overload. The inference is well-supported by the collective data.

results.result: The widespread aggregation caused by ATM loss follows a predictable pattern overlapping with neurodegenerative disorder aggregation, supporting the hypothesis that disrupted protein homeostasis is an important disease mechanism in ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T).
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 connect the current findings to A-T disease mechanisms. C130 is supported by citation to recent work. C131 is established knowledge. C132 is supported by the overlap with disease-associated aggregates (C82-C83) and the characteristics of aggregating proteins (supersaturation, LLPS propensity). This is an important translational implication of the work.

results.result: Other genotoxic conditions including chemotherapeutic TOP poisons have similar impacts on protein aggregation as ATM loss, pointing to a broader link between DNA damage and loss of protein homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134 are supported by the similar aggregation patterns observed across different genotoxic conditions (C5-C7, C23-C36) and the overlap in aggregating proteins and their characteristics. This is a key conclusion extending the findings beyond ATM to a general principle linking genotoxic stress to proteostatic stress.

results.result: TDP1 inhibition and PARP1-3 inhibition do not increase protein aggregation, but PARP inhibition can reduce CPT-induced aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27 and C32 show negative results that help define the specificity of the genotoxic stress response. Claim C33 shows that PARP inhibition can suppress aggregation, consistent with the role of PARylation in LLPS regulation (C121). These are important controls and mechanistic insights.

results.result: Background knowledge establishing that ATM loss impairs DNA damage response and causes A-T (characterized by neurodegeneration and cancer predisposition), that ATM loss is associated with protein aggregation, and that protein homeostasis is maintained by quality control systems that can be overwhelmed during stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C14-C22, C31 represent established scientific knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These provide essential background context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and accurate.
